characterList.description: Curly hair, glasses, often wears a plaid shirt.
characterList.name: Scientist 1 (Nick)

characterList.description: Wavy hair parted on the side, glasses.
characterList.name: Scientist 2 (Jonathan)

characterList.description: Woman with tied hair and glasses. Appears multiple times.
characterList.name: Researcher

characterList.description: Man in a hat and long coat.
characterList.name: Editor

characterList.description: Man wearing a lab coat and glasses.
characterList.name: Librarian

characterList.description: Multiple figures representing scientists, citizens, etc. appear throughout.
characterList.name: People

content_metadata.description: A persuasive exploration of the benefits and necessity of open access in scientific research, utilizing personal stories, historical context, and future aspirations to advocate for change.

qAndA.answer: Paper airplanes are used in Scene 1 to illustrate the circulation and sharing of research made possible by open access.
qAndA.question: What visual symbol is used to represent the flow of research enabled by open access?

qAndA.answer: The librarian looks shocked and overwhelmed as he receives the expensive bill, visually portraying the financial strain of rising journal costs.
qAndA.question: What does the librarian’s expression convey in Scene 3?

qAndA.answer: Nick’s wife's medical emergency and his inability to access critical research articles while in the hospital (Scene 6) triggered his realization of the urgent need for open access.
qAndA.question: What specific event caused Nick to change his mind about the importance of open access?

qAndA.answer: A melting iceberg symbolizes the shrinking relevance of traditional prestige metrics and the need for the scientific community to adapt to a more open system.
qAndA.question: What visual metaphor is used in Scene 10 to represent the declining influence of traditional scientific publishing practices?

qAndA.answer: Jonathan urges graduate students to initiate conversations about open access with their research teams and principal investigators, advocating for a shift in publishing practices.
qAndA.question: What specific action does Jonathan encourage graduate students to take in Scene 12?

activities.description: Nick and Jonathan stand, discussing open access.
Paper airplanes circle a globe. A researcher reads papers.
Two researchers brainstorm with paper airplanes.
Nick, Jonathan, and a third researcher discuss open access.

characterInteraction.description: Nick and Jonathan discuss the value and purpose of open access.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Sets the stage for understanding the concept and significance of open access.

narrativeProgression.description: Definition of open access.
Open access makes research globally available.
Open access encourages collaboration and makes research more valuable.

scenes.thematicElements: Importance of open access, benefits of shared knowledge, collaboration in research.
scenes.title: Introduction to Open Access

videoEditingDetails.description: Simple animations (text, drawing, color changes) throughout the scene.
Smooth transitions between visual ideas.

activities.description: Editor discusses the history of scientific publishing, emphasizing high costs.
Editor explains the traditional journal submission and publishing process. Animations illustrate the steps.
Editor notes the system worked, but changes are occurring. Visual transition to a question mark and papers with hourglasses.

characterInteraction.description: Editor talks to the viewer, explaining the historical model.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Provides background on traditional publishing practices and costs.

narrativeProgression.description: High cost of traditional publishing.
Detailed explanation of the submission, review, and printing process.
Acknowledging the system's past success, but hinting at change.

scenes.thematicElements: History of scientific publishing, cost of publishing, the role of journals.
scenes.title: History of Scientific Publishing

videoEditingDetails.description: Smooth transitions between explanations and corresponding visuals.
Use of fast-forward animation during the printing press sequence.

activities.description: Nick and Jonathan explain the two main changes: digitization and journal price increases. Visuals illustrate these changes.
Librarian receives an expensive bill, representing rising journal costs.
Nick and Jonathan express frustration with the rising costs.

characterInteraction.description: Nick and Jonathan discuss the changes. The librarian is shown struggling with the bill.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Highlights the current challenges faced by institutions due to rising publication costs.

narrativeProgression.description: Digitization and journal price increases.
The burden of rising costs on librarians and institutions.
Reaching the point of absurdity with high journal subscription costs.

props.name: Stack of books with price tags

scenes.thematicElements: Digitization of research, escalating journal prices, financial burden on institutions.
scenes.title: Challenges in Modern Scientific Publishing

videoEditingDetails.description: Split-screen to show digitization and price increase happening simultaneously.
Fast-paced animations for paper turning into digital data and prices increasing.

activities.description: Nick argues that journals don't produce the content; researchers do the work. Visuals depict researchers doing experiments, writing, and reviewing.
Nick expresses frustration with the system's irrationality. Visuals show researchers buried in papers.
Nick criticizes the restricted access to publicly funded research. Visuals depict a building representing the government and taxpayers. A researcher tries to access research but is denied.

characterInteraction.description: Nick is the main speaker, addressing the viewer. Researchers, reviewers, and the public are depicted visually.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Emphasizes the ethical issues and inefficiencies within the current publishing model.

narrativeProgression.description: Journals don't produce content, yet control access.
The system is illogical and contradicts the spirit of scientific progress.
Publicly funded research is inaccessible to the public, creating a profound ethical problem.

scenes.thematicElements: Researcher exploitation, irrationality of the current system, public funding and public access.
scenes.title: Critique of the Current System

videoEditingDetails.description: Transition from individual researchers to a pile of papers, emphasizing the volume of research.
The government building and research locked in a box symbolize restricted access.

activities.description: Nick and Jonathan discuss how access problems impact students and researchers, especially in less wealthy nations. Visuals depict a student denied access to research and professors limited in their teaching.
Jonathan recounts his experience as a student encountering access barriers and the lack of awareness regarding the underlying system.

characterInteraction.description: Nick and Jonathan discuss the issues. Student and Professor are shown struggling with access limitations.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Highlights the broader societal implications of restricted access on education and research.

narrativeProgression.description: Impact on students and researchers, especially in developing countries.
Lack of awareness and acceptance of the system as the norm.

scenes.thematicElements: Education, global research equity, systemic barriers to access.
scenes.title: Impact of Access Limitations

videoEditingDetails.description: Cubicle maze visual symbolizes restricted access and the complexity of the system.

activities.description: Nick explains his initial skepticism about open access.

Nick tells a story about his wife's medical emergency, his desperate attempts to access research, and being blocked by paywalls. He expresses frustration at the lack of access to critical information.

characterInteraction.description: Nick recounts the story to the viewer. The wife, doctors, and Nick are shown in the hospital scene.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Humanizes the issue by connecting it to a real-life scenario, illustrating the broader implications of restricted access.

narrativeProgression.description: Nick was initially unconvinced about the importance of open access.
The medical emergency and inability to access critical research papers made him realize the urgent need for open access.

scenes.thematicElements: Personal impact of restricted access, healthcare, urgency of open access.
scenes.title: A Personal Story of Restricted Access

videoEditingDetails.description: Transition to a somber blue color scheme during the hospital scene.
The heart rate monitor adds a sense of urgency.

activities.description: Nick explains that he paid for numerous articles during his wife's medical crisis.
Nick points out the flaw: you only discover an article's relevance after paying, with no refunds. Visuals depict Nick buying articles and discarding irrelevant ones.

characterInteraction.description: Nick addresses the viewer, highlighting the personal financial burden.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Illustrates the inefficiencies and personal impact of the current paywall system.

narrativeProgression.description: Nick spent a significant amount of money on articles.
The core problem: paying without knowing relevance, leading to waste.

scenes.thematicElements: Pay-per-view model, financial burden on individuals, lack of transparency.
scenes.title: The Cost of Paywalls

videoEditingDetails.description: The hole in the ground visualizes the financial drain of buying irrelevant articles.

activities.description: Nick clarifies that open access proponents are not against publishing costs or for everything being free.
Nick advocates for a system where publicly funded research is openly accessible. Visuals depict a contrast between open access and restricted publishing models.

characterInteraction.description: Nick directly addresses the viewer, challenging their assumptions and advocating for change.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Clarifies the goals of open access and advocates for an equitable system.

narrativeProgression.description: Open access is not about everything being free; it's about a more responsible use of public funding.
Calling for a system where publicly funded research is openly available, benefiting society as a whole.

scenes.thematicElements: Misconceptions about open access, public funding, societal benefits of open research.
scenes.title: Advocating for Open Access

videoEditingDetails.description: Split-screen contrasts the open and restricted publishing models.
Arrows visually demonstrate the flow of taxpayer funding.

activities.description: Jonathan explains the two key components of open access: free to read and free to reuse. Visuals illustrate these concepts.
Jonathan highlights the potential of open access to enable data mining and collaborative research across disciplines.

characterInteraction.description: Jonathan explains the concepts to the viewer. Researchers are shown collaborating and using digital tools.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Illustrates the transformative potential of open access for research and innovation.

narrativeProgression.description: The two core principles: free access and free reuse.
Open access enables data mining and collaborative research, leading to breakthroughs.

scenes.thematicElements: Open access principles, data mining, interdisciplinary research.
scenes.title: The Components and Potential of Open Access

videoEditingDetails.description: Split-screen to demonstrate 'free to read' and 'free to reuse.'
Animation shows data extracted from papers, connecting across disciplines.

activities.description: Jonathan explains the limitations of current copyright restrictions, preventing large-scale data mining.
Nick discusses the slow pace of change in scientific culture. Visuals depict scientists clinging to a shrinking iceberg, representing traditional practices.

characterInteraction.description: Jonathan explains the limitations, and then Nick addresses the viewer, emphasizing the cultural barrier.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Addresses the cultural and systemic barriers to embracing open access in the scientific community.

narrativeProgression.description: Current copyright restrictions hinder innovation.
Scientists' attachment to traditional prestige metrics hinders the adoption of open access.

scenes.thematicElements: Copyright restrictions, resistance to change, prestige metrics in science.
scenes.title: Cultural Resistance and Need for Change

videoEditingDetails.description: Melting iceberg symbolizes the decline of traditional practices and the need for change.

activities.description: Nick challenges the status quo, arguing for experimentation with different publishing models. Visuals show locked boxes representing traditional publishing and people experimenting with alternative systems.
Nick suggests corporations may lead the way and advocates for openness as the future.

characterInteraction.description: Nick addresses the viewer, challenging them to consider the future of scientific publishing.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Encourages exploration of new models and warns against stagnation in outdated practices.

narrativeProgression.description: The current system is not necessarily optimal; we need to explore alternatives.
Corporations might be faster to adapt, leaving traditional publishers behind.

scenes.thematicElements: Need for innovation, adaptation to change, corporate vs. academic publishing.
scenes.title: Experimenting with New Models

videoEditingDetails.description: Juxtaposition of traditional boxes with open, accessible systems.
The skull symbolizes the potential 'death' of old publishing models.

activities.description: Jonathan emphasizes the importance of graduate students starting conversations about open access with their research teams.
Nick expresses his belief that open access benefits both researchers and the broader scientific community by accelerating discovery.

characterInteraction.description: Jonathan and Nick address both the viewer and the graduate students represented visually.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Positions graduate students as potential agents of change within the scientific community.

narrativeProgression.description: Graduate students have the power to initiate conversations and influence research practices.
Open access benefits everyone by accelerating scientific discovery and sharing knowledge.

scenes.thematicElements: Call to action, graduate student engagement, benefits of open access for researchers.
scenes.title: The Role of Graduate Students

videoEditingDetails.description: Animation shows papers circulating and reaching a wider audience, highlighting the spread of knowledge.

climax.description: Nick's personal story about being denied access to vital medical research creates an emotional climax, driving home the urgency and real-world implications of open access.

storylines.description: A persuasive exploration of the benefits and necessity of open access in scientific research, utilizing personal stories, historical context, and future aspirations to advocate for change.

content_metadata.title: Unlocking Access: The Case for Open Science

trimmingSuggestions.description: The extended animation of the traditional publishing process could be shortened to maintain momentum.
The iceberg metaphor could be more visually dynamic to enhance the sense of urgency.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Open Access is free, immediate, online,
availability of research articles with full reuse rights.
This is about, first of all, making all this content available for anyone
wherever they are in the world to read and access and build upon
so people can do interesting things and work in new ways with the material
to really make the research literature much more valuable.
The history of the model is really publishing scientific,
manual scripts, especially ones with complex, detailed color figures, was expensive.
And so if you wanted your article distributed broadly and widely,
you sent it to one of these journals and then they would manage the review process
and the communications with reviewers and revisions and eventually something would be accepted
in they handled the type setting and the printing and the distribution of your scientific work.
And it worked great. It science progressed pretty well and it became a good way to distribute scientific papers.
And what's changed is really two things in essence.
First is digitization. You can now do everything electronically instead of printing it.
And the second is that the journals started ratcheting up the price of subscriptions to many of their journals.
And so those two things came sort of to a head where it's become almost the theater of the absurd
with the amount that some journals want, libraries to pay to subscribe to the journal.
Research has shown that journal prices have actually outpaced inflation by over 250% over the past 30 years.
They're over 15 entire academic disciplines where the average price for one journal is over $1,000 for one subscription for one year.
Yeah, in chemistry, the average title is $4,227 and physics $3,649.
And it even goes down into like agriculture is still over 1,000 and geology and botany all over 1,000.
And those are just the averages. There's like the way out there. There's a journal called Ketcher Heatrin that's $40,000.
The journals aren't producing the material. The journals don't employ the people who write the papers.
They don't even employ the people who review the papers. And it doesn't make a lot of sense in terms of what science is supposed to be about.
It's supposed to be about discovering new things and spreading that knowledge around.
It's so irrational to think that these scientists like me are paid by the government to do research and to discover things and distribute that.
And then, you know, two years of work by 20 people is going to be compressed into a paper and then not made available to people.
It just doesn't make any sense.
Yeah, so I think this problem of access to research is one that people run into all the time.
But it's not one that they sort of realize. I know when I was a student, whenever I would be doing research and come across a great abstract and not have access to it,
I just sort of moved on and thought, you know, well, this is the way it is.
There's, you know, I didn't really realize that there was a system behind this.
You know, that was causing me to not have access. And I think students' educations literally depend on access to the journal literature.
I mean, professors can only teach what they have access to.
If you look at less wealthy countries, like low and middle income countries, they're really, really struggle to get access.
And, you know, so that's a real impediment that prevents researchers in those countries from being able to contribute fully or do world class research.
I mean, I was not even with this lack of access and even with my brother starting the public library of science, I wasn't convinced.
I didn't understand why this was a big deal.
And then we had a family medical emergency and I was up at three in the middle of the night in a hospital next to my wife in the hospital room,
surfing the web on the crappy hospital wireless internet.
And I was trying to find out information about a particular medical treatment and I couldn't get access to the damn papers.
And our doctors didn't know the answer to these particular questions.
And we needed to decide about what to do with this medical treatment.
And here I was a trained scientist with the ability to read and interpret and understand many of these papers.
And I couldn't get them.
And I just, that was the moment for me. I was like, you've got to be kidding me.
Here's the, what the problem comes down to in most cases. And it gets in the hospital room, I paid. I bought dozens of articles.
The problem is that you don't know which article is relevant until after you pay for it.
The abstracts don't always make it clear what is contained in the paper.
So there was no return policy, right? I couldn't buy it and then say, this is wrong. I'm giving it back.
So now you're going to spend $1,200 to just find out if possibly they're relevant.
I mean, if you do that every day, you're in a big hole.
It's not, I'm not, you know, some communist saying everything should be free. And, you know, I don't believe in corporations.

Nobody is saying that publishing is free. What people are saying is that we need to work on models where the government that is already paying for the research and is then paying for the subscriptions and is then paying for the indirect costs for the libraries.
I mean, in the end, taxpayers and the government are paying for this. So why can't we do it in a way where the knowledge is distributed broadly as opposed to the knowledge is restricted?
So there are two components of open access. The first is that articles are available for free to read so that you don't hit that paywall when you click to read the full tax.

The second part of the definition that's every bit as important is that the articles come with full reuse rights so that scientists and researchers can build an entire new tier of tools on top of the research literature.
And those new tools can interact with these articles, right? They can mind the articles. They can find relationships.
You know, they can find snippets of genetic code that are mentioned in multiple papers or different phrases or concepts that are referenced in a biology paper and a chemistry paper.
You know, that individual researchers would never be able to uncover because they can't read this many articles.
So if you actually wanted to do that, you couldn't because you would have to negotiate individual rights with every single publisher in order to do that.
In an open access world, all this information would be open on the internet for free and people would have unrestricted rights, you know, to do that kind of data mining.
I think the main impediment is the incredibly slow movement of scientific cultural practices.
I mean, I think, you know, scientists, despite being great explorers in terms of knowledge are sort of very conservative in terms of changing their practices.
Lots of the community says, oh, yeah, I support openness, but I want a nature paper.
That sort of reliance upon, you know, impact factor and the name of the journal does allow some journals to not respond to the community pressure towards openness.
The scientific publishing model that we have now, there's no evidence that it is optimal.
We need to experiment with all sorts of different scientific publishing systems.
Corporations may figure that out before governments do.
I'm very open to whoever is going to come up with creative solutions to these issues.
I view it much more as scientists and scientific publishers are slow to change.
Some of them are going to be left in the dirt because openness is clearly the future and the creative ones are going to survive.
It's really important. They graduate students, you know, start these conversations with the research teams, their PIs, you know, just let them know that it's something that they care about.
And, you know, there's a real benefit to researchers, to graduate students by doing this, right?
Because the more people that see your work, the more people can build upon it, then they'll say you.
It's not just good for the person that can read your paper. It's also good for you.
I believe that scientific knowledge spreads and increases best if there are no restrictions on access to the knowledge that has been generated in other places.
I want the discovery of new scientific knowledge to happen faster. And openness helps accelerate that.

Even if for your own reasons you need to publish in a subscription journal, there is this other option that even if you don't publish in an open access journal that you can still make, you know, the text of the article itself freely available so that people can at least read it and get access to it.
